claims.text: For supported Pd catalysts in aerobic oxidation reactions, the density of metal–oxide interfacial sites is the key factor governing selectivity.
A moderate controlled oxidation pretreatment generates Pd–oxide interfacial sites.
Pd–oxide interfacial sites facilitate targeted electron transfer.
Interfacial electron transfer tunes the adsorption of reaction intermediates.
The resulting adsorption changes enhance formation of the desired oxygenated product.
The as-received commercial Pd/Al2O3 catalyst has a mixed and largely uncontrolled Pd oxidation-state distribution.
Pretreatment in air at 150 °C for 2 hours partially oxidizes Pd and creates well-distributed Pd/PdO interfacial regions.
Hydrogen pretreatment produces a predominantly metallic Pd surface.
Air pretreatment at 300 °C produces a fully or over-oxidized Pd surface.
Nanoscale Pd/PdO interfaces modify the Pd d-band structure.
Modification of the Pd d-band changes the adsorption energies of reaction intermediates.
A balance between metallic Pd and Pd oxide creates synergistic interfacial sites that accelerate electron transfer and alter adsorption.
Predominantly metallic and over-oxidized catalysts lack the proposed interfacial synergy.
Loss of the proposed interfacial synergy lowers selectivity for the desired oxidation product.
The catalyst pretreated at 150 °C in air will have higher benzaldehyde selectivity or yield than the hydrogen-treated and 300 °C air-treated catalysts.
The catalyst pretreated at 150 °C in air will maintain similar or improved benzyl alcohol conversion rates.
The proposed interfacial effect is expected to dominate for Pd on inert high-surface-area oxide supports at approximately 100–150 °C under dilute-feed oxidation conditions.
Support interactions and particle-size distributions may influence the observed catalytic performance.
XPS, TEM, and DRIFTS can quantify the extent and distribution of Pd/PdO interfaces and associated adsorbed intermediates.
